title: Dublin, Ohio Moves to Rezone Its 210-Acre Metro Center as Mixed-Use
author: CRE News Staff
excerpt: Dublin, Ohio P&Z reviewed draft design standards for Metro Center rezoning Sept. 17. Over 90 acres of the 210-acre Columbus-area park may become mixed-use.

body:
Dublin, Ohio's Planning and Zoning Commission reviewed draft design standards on September 17 for Metro Center, the city's first major suburban office park. The rezoning process — covering more than 90 acres of surface parking across a 210-acre campus — is expected to reach a Dublin City Council vote in winter 2026-27.

## The Case for Change: 90 Acres of Asphalt in One of Ohio's Strongest Suburbs

Metro Center was Dublin's original planned office park, developed from the 1970s through the 1990s along the Sawmill Road corridor north of I-270. It remains one of the larger concentrations of suburban office inventory in the Columbus metro, but more than 90 of its 210 total acres are surface parking — roughly 7,700 parking spaces built around commuters who drove in, sat down, and left. That model has been losing relevance for decades.

Dublin began formal planning to transform Metro Center after Dublin City Council adopted the [Metro Center Revitalization Plan and Design Framework](https://telldublin.dublinohiousa.gov/metro-center-revitalization) on December 9, 2024. The plan earned the Specialized Plan Award from the Ohio Chapter of the American Planning Association in September 2025, a signal that regional planners found the approach credible.

The city's stated goal: reimagine Metro Center as a walkable, mixed-use district with housing, retail, restaurants, public parks, and expanded trail and cycling connections — closer in character to what Dublin built at Bridge Street than what Metro Center has been since it opened.

## What Happened September 17, 2026

On September 17, 2026, Dublin city staff presented draft design guidelines and a proposed zoning framework for the Metro Center area to the Planning and Zoning Commission for the first time. The meeting was a work session, a format in which staff introduces draft materials to commissioners without a formal vote. Commissioners offered early feedback; no recommendation was made.

[ABC6 WSYX](https://abc6onyourside.com/news/local/dublin-eyes-major-transformation-of-metro-center-as-walkable-mixed-use-district) covered Dublin's Metro Center ambitions before the September 17 session. [CWColumbus](https://cwcolumbus.com/news/local/dublin-eyes-major-transformation-of-metro-center-as-walkable-mixed-use-district) reported on the same vision. Both characterized the transformation as one of the most significant planning efforts Dublin has taken on since the Bridge Street District.

Additional Planning and Zoning Commission meetings are scheduled for fall 2026 before a formal recommendation. Dublin City Council is expected to consider the rezoning and accompanying design standards in winter 2026-27.

## What the Draft Plan Proposes

The Metro Center Revitalization framework envisions nine new zoning districts covering different character types within the 210-acre area. The draft standards govern building types, massing, height, and how new construction connects to the public realm.

Core elements include:

- **Surface parking conversion**: More than 90 acres of asphalt — about 43 percent of the total site — representing the primary development capacity under the new rules
- **Mixed uses**: Housing, retail, and food-and-beverage uses on parcels currently zoned for office only
- **Trail and pedestrian links**: Expanded connections to Dublin's path network and toward Bridge Street, Dublin's already-built mixed-use model nearby
- **Design standards**: Streetscape, building massing, and open space requirements designed to create a coherent sense of place across what is now an auto-oriented campus

The rezoning does not obligate any existing owner to redevelop. It changes what is permitted, not what is required. Existing tenants with long-term leases would continue on current terms; the practical effect unfolds parcel by parcel as leases roll and owners weigh their options.

## Bridge Street: The Nearby Template

Dublin's closest analog for what Metro Center could become is the Bridge Street District, developed starting in the early 2010s along Bridge Street east of Sawmill. That district now includes multiple residential buildings, a Hilton hotel, restaurants, retailers, and the pedestrian Bridge Park spanning the Scioto River. Crawford Hoying, Edwards Companies, and M/I Homes — all active across Central Ohio — led major phases of Bridge Street.

Dublin's proximity narrative for developers is direct: a comparable mixed-use transformation happened nearby; Metro Center is the next opportunity at larger scale. The comparison has limits. Bridge Street largely built on land that lacked active tenants. Metro Center has a functioning, if undersized, office market. The transition will be more gradual. But the rezoning framework being developed allows developers to acquire parcels ahead of any lease rollovers and before City Council acts.

## What This Means for Columbus Real Estate Professionals

**Suburban office landlords in Dublin**: The Council vote is several months away, but land acquisition decisions typically lead city action by a year or more. Owners of older Metro Center buildings carrying below-market occupancy may find the rezoning creates an exit path — a land-value premium over distressed-office comps that currently dominates their alternatives.

**Residential and mixed-use developers**: More than 90 acres of surface parking represents low-demolition-cost land in one of Central Ohio's strongest residential corridors. The final density allowances in the design standards will determine whether projects pencil out. Bridge Street precedent suggests Dublin is prepared to allow meaningful floor-area ratios when projects meet its design standards.

**Affordable housing operators**: Dublin has historically imposed minimal affordability requirements in large mixed-use approvals. Whether inclusionary standards appear in the Metro Center zoning — and at what income thresholds — has not been disclosed in publicly available materials reviewed for this story.

**Columbus metro investors broadly**: Metro Center sits inside the I-270 beltway in a submarket with consistently strong residential demand, proximity to corporate campuses, and access to COTA service on the Sawmill corridor. A successful rezoning would represent one of the largest planned mixed-use redevelopment opportunities to emerge in the Columbus suburbs in a decade. The next hard date is the Dublin City Council vote, expected in winter 2026-27.
